title: Harmony Inn, slowing down around 1950, no street parades
summary: He played three nights a week at the Harmony Inn in the 1940s, slowed down around 1950, and says all his jobs were sit-in jobs, not parades.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Then Mealy Bones I played by the Harmony Inn. Oh yes.
I might have even heard you down there. I heard that band. Maybe you were in there one time.
I didn't even know you. But this guy played the piano. He died too. I just remember his name now.

Walter. Walter. Walter Decoe. Oh, is he dead? I didn't know for sure if he's dead. Yeah, he's dead. I knew he wasn't playing anymore. They told me he was dead. That's what I heard. Yeah, I've never heard for sure if he died. Lawrence Torkum. Yeah. I knew him.
Emile Bones. I worked down there quite a while. At the Harmony Inn.
Three nights a week I played. Was that in the 1940's?
Yeah, that was in the 40's. When did you quit the music business? You really haven't quit yet I guess. You still have your drums? No, I'm coming back on the chair.

I have a set of drums and everything. I have a good set of drums. And, well I slacked down say around 1949 I think. Or 1950. Yeah, around 1950. It ain't too far back. No, no. You don't lose too much practice.
No, no. You learn something that you really know you never forget like that. No, no, you never forget.
You'll be a little rusty but you come back strong. Yeah.
Yeah. Did you ever play much parade work on the streets?
No, I never played much parade in the streets. No. All my job was sit-in jobs.
